items.title: Man on ‘Mission’ to Handwrite Entire New Testament: ‘Anchor for My Soul’
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: "A starving man being invited into a banquet."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

It took Don Ashley about 210 hours over eight months and 15 days to write his own handwritten copy of the New Testament.

Ashley, a recently retired university administrator who relocated from Anchorage, Alaska, to farmland in Arkansas, posted to social media this month that he’d just completed the project — an endeavor he said he began “on a whim” on Jan. 5.

View on Threads

But what started as an impulse quickly turned into what he called “a mission.”

“In all these life transitions,” he told CBN News, “this really served as an anchor for my soul.”

The idea, he explained, was born out of a work trip to the Society of Biblical Literature, a 146-year-old learning society dedicated to the academic study of the Bible and other ancient writings.

When he was at the meeting in San Diego, Ashley saw a display of the Dead Sea Scrolls, a collection of roughly 1,000 ancient Jewish manuscripts dating from the 3rd century B.C. to the 1st century A.D. They were discovered in the 1940s and 50s.

“I was so impressed by the artistry required … that I wanted to experience something about what the ancient scribes experienced,” Ashley said.

The average American spends about two-and-a-half hours per day on social media. For teenagers, that number is nearly doubled, spending roughly five hours every day on social media apps. And 41% of teens who reported the highest social media use rated their mental health as poor or very poor, according to data from the American Psychological Association.

Much of that time is spent doomscrolling, a term that first broke into the American lexicon through Twitter in 2018 and was officially added to the dictionary in late 2020. The concept became pretty commonplace at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, when Americans of all ages were stuck at home spending an outsized portion of their days scrolling content on their phones.

Doomscrolling, for the uninitiated, is the habit of spending excessive time online browsing through often negative, depressing, and alarming news content. Needless to say, dedicating a great deal of energy to that kind of content can quickly become distressing and take a significant toll on users’ mental health — particularly if they have no belief in a sovereign God who promises to work together all things to the good of those who love Him (Romans 8:28).

As for Ashley, he felt handwriting the Bible was a better, more profitable use of his time.

“I think the idea that, instead of doomscrolling, maybe you could do something more useful with your time,” he said. “The world is so fast-paced now, maybe it appeals to the idea of slowing down.”

The process was deeply cathartic for Ashley, who is currently recovering from a significant back surgery. He likened the project, in a spiritual sense, to “a starving man being invited into a banquet.”

“I made mistakes on this page and I didn’t worry too much about the mistakes,” he said, holding up a page from his journal where he’d marked over some errors. “I just lined through them and kept going.”

When it was all said and done, Ashley noted that — while he didn’t walk away with any new theological revelations — it was spiritually encouraging to physically experience Scripture in a new way.

“I’ve experienced the Bible with my mind for my whole career and since my initial conversion experience in 1985,” he said, “but I wanted to experience it with my fingers. Putting a pen to paper is a different experience than reading it.”

Watch our full conversation with Ashley in the video above.

items.title: First Liberty: Minnesota County Has ‘Essentially Criminalized Being Amish’
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Wow.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

The Amish community in Minnesota is pushing back amid claims of unfair government policies that purportedly fail to offer religious accommodations — and even reportedly led to one Amish man’s arrest.

First Liberty attorney Ryan Gardner said his firm is representing two Amish congregations in Mille Lacs County, Minnesota, arguing the county itself has “essentially criminalized being Amish.”

“As you might know, the Amish community lives by a pretty strict set of religious principles, and many of those involve not being involved in technology,” Gardner said. “And kind of keeping to themselves … they want to be able to live according to their religious beliefs, and a lot of what those beliefs require, frankly … to be set apart from modern society.”

According to First Liberty, problems began for these congregations during COVID-19, when county officials reportedly implemented a new permitting system for building structures and homes.

“It went from a paper form to an electronic form,” Gardner said. “As you might imagine, the Amish don’t really use electronic forms or the internet, so this was a significant problem, and they had no alternative for a long time.”

With no other option for simply getting clearance to build homes, he said “a lot of the people in these congregations just proceeded to build anyways because they didn’t have a choice.”

Gardner said Mille Lacs County did eventually change the policy to make a paper option available, but added there is an additional $50 fee for requesting permitting on paper.

“Pretty much the only people who are actually using that are the Amish, and so now they’re having to pay a special fee just to even start the permitting process,” the lawyer said. “And once they get in, there are more problems because they’re trying to impose all kinds of modern requirements that are just inconsistent with the Amish way of life.”

Gardner said officials have been so hard on the Amish that they even put one man in jail “for the crime of building and living in his home.”

“This particular individual had been living in his home for something like five years and then, suddenly, he’s criminally cited for it, and he goes to court, and he’s convicted,” the lawyer said. “And he is … immediately taken to jail.”

Gardner said it is “ludicrous” and “extreme” to prosecute someone for such a “petty” offense, and added that such a reaction is rare. He added that the Amish had purportedly tried to go to the county to work the issue out but were “met with hostility.”

“Here’s the kicker in all of this,” he continued, “Built into the very ordinance that the county is enforcing here is a provision that gives the county discretion to give exemptions to these requirements to anybody that it wants.”

First Liberty sent a letter to the county recently demanding they stop enforcement actions against the Amish, especially considering warrants that are currently out for others. They’re also looking for an exemption that would settle the issue once and for all, noting that, from his perspective, the Amish build insanely safe structures.

Mille Lacs County told CBN News that lawyers cannot comment on ongoing cases.

items.title: Gen Z and Millennials Are Drinking Less. But Gen X Definitely Isn’t.
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: Mocktails have their own section on the menu now, and “sober curious” is a personality. The generations that made that happen are finally showing up in the data. So is the one that didn’t. Alcohol use among U.S. adults has fallen for the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic began
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Mocktails have their own section on the menu now, and “sober curious” is a personality. The generations that made that happen are finally showing up in the data. So is the one that didn’t.

Alcohol use among U.S. adults has fallen for the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic began, according to a new Keck Medicine of USC study published Monday in Annals of Internal Medicine. Gen Z and millennials led the drop.

From 2022 to 2024, the share of adults who drank at all fell by nearly 2 percent. Heavy drinking fell by more than 8 percent.

Gen Z had the biggest decline in drinking at all, down more than 5 percent. Millennials had the biggest decline in heavy drinking: 17 percent in two years.

But Gen X adults 50 to 64 went the other way.

In that age group, alcohol use rose nearly 4 percent between 2018 and 2024. Heavy drinking rose by more than 36 percent.

“Heavy drinking among ages 50-64 is up by more than a third since 2018, a concerning trend because this age group faces some of the greatest risks of harm from alcohol, including cirrhosis and alcohol-related cancers,” said Dr. Brian P. Lee, the Keck Medicine hepatologist who led the study.

That risk isn’t abstract. Alcohol accounts for roughly half of all liver-related deaths, according to Lee, and alcohol-associated cirrhosis is now the leading cause of liver transplants. The study drew on more than 100,000 respondents, who answered privately online instead of over the phone, and it follows Lee’s earlier research showing drinking climbed during the pandemic and kept climbing for two years after. Overall, Americans are still drinking more than they did before 2020.

What the study didn’t do is ask why younger adults are cutting back. The researchers point to changing social attitudes toward alcohol as one possible explanation.

“It’s encouraging to see alcohol use decline for the first time since the start of the pandemic,” Lee said. “However, use remains above pre-pandemic levels and certain groups continue to have concerning trends.”

The mocktail menu is working. Somebody tell your parents.

items.title: A New Adaption of ‘East of Eden’—Please Read the Book First
items.author: Henry T. Edmondson III
items.summary:
Henry T. Edmondson III

Will the Netflix release—as good as it might be—give people an easy opt-out of tackling the novel?
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Henry T. Edmondson III

To ask someone, “What is your all-time favorite novel?” is a little unfair, especially if they are an active reader. A more reasonable question might be, “What are your top-five favorite novels?” For me, one of the five will always be East of Eden (1952) by John Steinbeck. I had the privilege of reading and discussing it with several other people for the first time in the Salinas Valley of central California, Steinbeck’s home and the setting of the novel. He is the author of The Grapes of Wrath (1939), Of Mice and Men (1937), Cannery Row (1945), and the Winter of Our Discontent (1961). He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1962 and thought East of Eden was his most important novel, even though The Grapes of Wrath has been his most celebrated work.

Life East of Eden

I found the book overwhelming, so I wasn’t surprised when a student of mine said he had recently read East of Eden, and it had “changed his life.” Steinbeck’s novel is a retelling of the Genesis account of evil entering paradise and, consequently, those who made it their home were ordered to leave by the Eastern Gate, which was then guarded by a sword-wielding angel to prevent reentry. The novel also deals with the reality of evil, the freedom to choose good or evil, and the possibility of overcoming evil and experiencing redemption over time.

After their transgression, “at the breezy time of the day,” Adam and Eve were confronted by the Lord God. They then hid themselves “among the trees of the garden.”

The Lord God called to the man, and said to him, “Where are you?” He said, “I heard the sound of you in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; and I hid myself.”  

God then asked the telling question, “Who told you that you were naked?” The Lord already knew the answer to his follow-up query, “Have you eaten from the tree of which I had forbidden you to eat?” In what might have been the first recorded instance of “passing the buck,” Adam blamed Eve but implied that it was really God’s fault because he had given him Eve. Eve blamed the snake. The snake must have looked about and found no one else to blame.

The man said, “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate.” Then the Lord God said to the woman, “What is this that you have done?” The woman said, “The serpent tricked me, and I ate.”

After God pronounces the consequences for all three, he prepares them for their exit from paradise.

The Lord God made garments of skins for the man and for his wife, and clothed them. Then the Lord God said, “See, the man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil; and now, he might reach out his hand and take also from the tree of life, and eat, and live forever”—therefore the Lord God sent him forth from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from which he was taken. He drove out the man; and at the east of the garden of Eden he placed the cherubim, and a sword flaming and turning to guard the way to the tree of life.

The Screen v. The Book

On October 1, a Netflix adaptation of East of Eden will premiere starring Florence Pugh, Mike Faist, and Christopher Abbott. Hoon Lee will play the important but understated role of the sage Chinese–American cook and housekeeper, Lee. This follows the 1955 film adaptation with James Dean and Julie Harris and the 1981 version with Timothy Bottoms and Jane Seymour.

Does this mean that those who might have read the book will not do so now? Will the Netflix release—as good as it might be—give people an easy opt-out of tackling the novel? For that matter, do the Jane Austen reimaginings and adaptations—from bad to very good—give those who might otherwise read the novels an off-ramp? 
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

In the dystopian classic Fahrenheit 451 (1953), books are prohibited, and the role of firemen is to burn any books that are discovered. The conclusion of the film offers hope as it depicts a rural sanctuary where each individual has memorized an entire classic book and, in so doing, preserves the book for everyone else. Among those books are Plato’s Republic, the Book of Ecclesiastes, the Book of Revelation, As You Like It (Shakespeare), The Wealth of Nations (Adam Smith), Leaves of Grass (Walt Whitman), and works by Marcus Aurelius, Einstein, and Gandhi.

Would that we had such commitment today! Keeping up with the assessments of American reading habits is like watching a slow-moving train wreck. Fewer than half of American adults now read for daily pleasure. The average American reads about two to five books per year, with roughly 40 to 50 percent of US adults reporting that they have not read a single book in the past twelve months; nor is it encouraging that 75 percent of Americans report that they have read at least “part of a book” over the course of a year. 

It gets worse, as not only are reading habits weak, but reading ability is steadily dropping as well. According to one study, about 130 million US adults (54 percent of those age sixteen to seventy-four) read below a sixth-grade level. Approximately forty-five million US adults are functionally illiterate, struggling to read below a fifth-grade level. 

In recent decades, faculty have found many of their students, even at the most prestigious universities, are overwhelmed by reading assignments—especially the Mt. Everest–like challenge of reading an entire book. There are at least two reasons: High schools, especially those afflicted by progressive educational ideas, tend to find it unreasonable to require students to read an entire book. Digital distractions, moreover, undermine the development of good reading habits. 

It seems, then, that in our day we don’t need the book-burning fireman destroying our books—we are taking care of that in our own way.

Squandering Leisure

This, then, is a modest plea to read Steinbeck’s novel before seeing the TV series. In his short but important book Leisure, the Basis of Culture, Josef Pieper warns that a society that does not know how to use leisure is a society at risk because a proper use of leisure is the irreplaceable foundation of a healthy culture. He worries that “unless we substitute true leisure for our hectic amusements, we will destroy our culture—and ourselves.” Pieper, an Aristotelian and a Thomist, logically extends the benefit of leisure, explaining that a proper use of leisure should lead to a “sense of wonder,” which is a step toward contemplation. Indeed, Aristotle opens his Metaphysics by noting the human inclination to wonder but also to nurture it. In On The Virtues of the Human Heart, Pieper explains that, as opposed to leisure, acēdia looks like laziness but is a more serious vice: acēdia is a denial of the experience of the goodness and grandeur of God. Pieper convincingly translates Psalm 46:10 not as “Be still and know that I am God” but rather as “Be at leisure and know that I am God.” All of this implies that a serious habit of reading is a dimension of leisure; short of that, the average person will be inhibited in their progress toward contemplation. There are practical benefits as well. When students ask me how they can learn to write better, I always tell them, “Read better.”

Steinbeck and Contemplation

So, what is the lesson here? Read Steinbeck and enjoy the beatific vision? Not quite. One of the reasons that purgatory makes sense is because, no matter how hard we try, it is unlikely that any of us will be prepared for God’s presence upon our passage from this life. We tend to think this is so because we may not shed our sinful nature in one easy step. Our wayward thoughts may not immediately dissipate. Except perhaps for saints, our passions may not be properly and wholly directed toward God. 

But our need for purgation may also involve our habits. In Thomistic moral philosophy, habits are not casual inclinations to grab Frappuccino from a Starbucks on the way to work. Rather, following Aristotle, a “habit” (ἕξις hexis) is a possession, a fixed disposition of character. To the degree these important components of character are deficient upon our passing, the cultivation of these essential habits is likely to be part of the purgatorial experience. 

Another problem with the small screen and the big screen is that, for the most part, they deprive us of the exercise and strengthening of our imagination, a companion faculty to our intellect, our memory, and our will. Aquinas taught that human beings cannot form abstract thoughts or intellectual concepts without the sensory images provided by the imagination, but if the imagination is weak, we are hobbled, just as we are when the will is weak. If it is healthy, our imagination is a far better director than anyone in Hollywood. 

Admittedly, cinema is an art form involving true artistry. Genuine film critics are some of the smartest people around, but then, they have read all the books. Shakespeare’s plays and Sophocles’s tragedies, moreover, were meant to be watched not read. But things have changed. Now, a sturdy habit of reading must come first. When I was growing up there were only two theaters in town—one showed regular movies, the other, movies you don’t want to see. Now, we are lucky enough to have as many as 500 TV channels, multiple theaters, and the opportunity to binge-watch a universe of digital entertainment. 

Will I, then, avoid the Netflix series? Perhaps, because so much of the book is fixed in my imagination, and no matter how good the screenplay may be, it cannot match the nuance and vivid images of the book I already relish. It’s the same reason I was reluctant to watch Project Hail Mary. My son, a science–fiction buff, had recommended the book, and although some of his recommendations are too technical for me, I was able to wrap my head around this one—and I couldn’t put it down. 

The Adaptation

Admittedly, the trailer to the Netflix adaptation of East of Eden is alluring. Will it be good? It will really depend on how well Florence Pugh can play a moral monster. The trailer cleverly begins with the early scene of the beaten and bloodied “Cathy” crawling to the doorstep of the Trask brothers. 

A dirty bundle of rags and mud was trying to worm its way up the steps. One skinny hand clawed slowly at the stairs. The other dragged helplessly. There was a caked face with cracked lips and eyes peering out of swollen, blackened lids. The forehead was laid open, oozing blood back into the matted hair (emphasis added).

Steinbeck’s choice of verbs recalls Canto 34 of the Inferno, where Virgil describes Satan as “the wicked worm that pierces through the world.” Steinbeck said of his character Cathy, “If you can believe in saints, you can believe that somebody can be all good, you’ve got to believe that somebody can be all bad.”

Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, the Gospel for today is incomparably rich and mysterious. First, we notice that peculiar question, “Who do the crowds say that I am?”
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
Ecclesiastes 3:1-11

For everything there is a season, and a time for every matter under heaven:

a time to be born, and a time to die;
a time to plant, and a time to pluck up what is planted;
a time to kill, and a time to heal;
a time to break down, and a time to build up;
a time to weep, and a time to laugh;
a time to mourn, and a time to dance;
a time to throw away stones, and a time to gather stones together;
a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing;
a time to seek, and a time to lose;
a time to keep, and a time to throw away;
a time to tear, and a time to sew;
a time to keep silence, and a time to speak;
a time to love, and a time to hate;
a time for war, and a time for peace.

What gain have the workers from their toil? I have seen the business that God has given to everyone to be busy with. He has made everything suitable for its time; moreover he has put a sense of past and future into their minds, yet they cannot find out what God has done from the beginning to the end.

Psalm
Psalm 144:1b and 2abc, 3-4

Blessed be the Lord, my rock,
    who trains my hands for war, and my fingers for battle;
my rock and my fortress,
    my stronghold and my deliverer,
my shield, in whom I take refuge,
    who subdues the peoples under me.
O Lord, what are human beings that you regard them,
    or mortals that you think of them?
They are like a breath;
    their days are like a passing shadow.

Gospel Reading
Luke 9: 18-22

Once when Jesus was praying alone, with only the disciples near him, he asked them, “Who do the crowds say that I am?” They answered, “John the Baptist; but others, Elijah; and still others, that one of the ancient prophets has arisen.” He said to them, “But who do you say that I am?” Peter answered, “The Messiah of God.”

He sternly ordered and commanded them not to tell anyone, saying, “The Son of Man must undergo great suffering, and be rejected by the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised.”

Reflection

Friends, the Gospel for today is incomparably rich and mysterious. First, we notice that peculiar question, “Who do the crowds say that I am?” No other religious figure or founder would ask such a question. This is the primordial and peculiar question of the Christian faith. It has to do with Jesus and who he is. 

The first group that “responds” is the general public: “John the Baptist; others, Elijah; still others, ‘One of the ancient prophets has arisen.’” A range of opinions—and all of them wrong.

Then that devastating question: “But who do you say that I am?” You who are closest to me, you whom I have chosen. But the disciples don’t speak. Are they afraid? Perhaps. Are they ignorant? Probably. 

Finally, Simon Peter speaks: “The Christ of God.” You are the Messiah, the anointed, the long-awaited Savior; but more to it, you are the Son of God, not just a human hero. This is the mystical faith that stands at the heart of Christianity. This is the standing or falling point. To hold this Petrine faith is to be a Christian; to deny it is not to be a Christian.
